Certified by Abstention: Distribution-Free Guarantees for
Chain-of-Thought Verifiers at Small Calibration Budgets

Arjun Balaji

Columbia University

arjun.balaji.02@gmail.com

Abstract

Signals that predict whether a chain-of-thought (CoT) trace is correct are compared by AUC, but deploying one requires a threshold with a guarantee. We ask what distribution-free selective guarantees deliver for CoT verifiers at realistic calibration budgets of tens to a few hundred labelled problems, using seven open models, five verifier signals and 37,000 graded traces. The central observation is validity by abstention: an (α,δ)(\alpha,\delta)-valid procedure that issues a certificate with probability PfireP_{\mathrm{fire}} bounds the failure probability of an issued certificate only by δ/Pfire\delta/P_{\mathrm{fire}}, so a certificate that rarely fires can be valid and wrong every time it is used. In a simulation with known risk the standard certificate fails in at most 0.3%0.3\% of calibration draws but in up to 69%69\% of those in which it fires. A certification floor and a lattice condition for Benjamini–Hochberg conformal selection explain why certificates abstain at these budgets, and the data bear them out: the standard certificate returns nothing or a large accepted set, and an unreadable residual-stream probe buys two to three times the coverage of the readable signals, an edge a cross-fitted reconstruction cannot recover linearly from the readable features. We then give a floor-started fixed-sequence certificate, valid without monotonicity assumptions, that covers more than the Bonferroni certificate on every model–signal pair and raises coverage at the non-vacuous target 0.75​π00.75\pi_{0} from 0.050.05 to 0.160.16, although the floor keeps absolute coverage small. Finally, a certificate cannot see what matters after deployment: under benchmark shift the error among accepted traces tracks the new task’s base error, and under best-of-nn selection against the verifier it rises past the target while the empirical failure frequency stays below δ\delta, because abstention absorbs the failures.

Introduction

Correctness of a language model’s reasoning can be predicted from cheap signals: the model’s token probabilities (Kadavath et al.,, 2022), linear probes on hidden states (Azaria and Mitchell,, 2023; Burns et al.,, 2023; Zhang et al.,, 2025), or readouts that decode intermediate activations into vocabulary space (nostalgebraist,, 2020; Belrose et al.,, 2023; Gurnee et al.,, 2026). Such verifier signals are compared almost exclusively by ranking metrics. A deployed verifier, however, is a threshold: traces scoring above it are accepted without further checking, and the operator needs to know how often an accepted trace is wrong.

Distribution-free methods promise this. Given a labelled calibration set, selective certificates (Geifman and El-Yaniv,, 2017), risk-controlling procedures (Bates et al.,, 2021; Angelopoulos et al.,, 2025) and conformal selection (Jin and Candès,, 2023; Gui et al.,, 2024) return an acceptance rule whose error is bounded with finite-sample validity under exchangeability alone. Their validity is not in question. What is rarely reported is what they deliver when labels are scarce, the target is non-vacuous, and the accepted traces are then optimized against. For CoT verification, calibration labels require graded solutions, and realistic budgets are tens to a few hundred problems. GSM8K’s automatic grading makes it a convenient stand-in for the tasks that motivate this regime, where each label costs an expert’s time; we therefore use 167–395 problems per model, the scale of a hand-graded set, and study larger budgets in simulation.

We study this regime with seven open-weight models (0.8B–8B parameters, three families), five verifier signals spanning the interpretability spectrum, and about 37,000 graded traces. The target is the selective error P⁡(wrong∣accepted)P(\text{wrong}\mid\text{accepted}). A target α\alpha is non-vacuous if it lies strictly below the model’s unconditional error rate π0\pi_{0}.

Contributions.

(1) Validity by abstention (§3). An (α,δ)(\alpha,\delta)-valid procedure that issues a certificate with probability PfireP_{\mathrm{fire}} bounds the failure probability of an issued certificate only by δ/Pfire\delta/P_{\mathrm{fire}} (Proposition 3). A certificate that rarely fires can therefore be valid and wrong every time it is used, and in a simulation with known risk the standard certificate does exactly that: it fails in at most 0.3%0.3\% of draws overall and in up to 69%69\% of the draws in which it fires, with a median overshoot of 4–12% of the target (§4.2). (2) Why certificates abstain at small budgets (§3, §4). A certification floor (Lemma 1) gives the smallest accepted calibration set that can certify a target, and a lattice condition (Proposition 2) decides exactly when BH conformal selection can reject anything. On seven models with 67–158 calibration problems the standard certificate is bimodal, abstaining or accepting a large set; at the non-vacuous target 0.75​π00.75\pi_{0} it fires in at most 10%10\% of calibration draws for 15 of 21 model–signal pairs, and below the boundary only one readable signal on one model reaches 10%10\% coverage. An unreadable residual probe buys two to three times the coverage of the readable signals at the boundary target and more below it, and a cross-fitted reconstruction shows that this edge is not linearly recoverable from the 119 readable features. The exact binomial bound is the tightest non-randomized bound on its statistic, so the lever is the multiplicity correction, not the bound. (3) A certificate that starts at the floor (§5). FS-floor is fixed-sequence Learn-then-Test (Angelopoulos et al.,, 2025) with thresholds fixed from the training split, a start at the floor of Lemma 1, and a start constant chosen by simulation before calibration. It is valid with no monotonicity assumption and covers more than the Bonferroni certificate on all 21 model–signal pairs at every target: at the non-vacuous target 0.75​π00.75\pi_{0} mean coverage rises from 0.050.05 to 0.160.16 and the certificate fires in 28%28\% rather than 10%10\% of calibration draws. The floor still binds, and a budget curve (Figure 2) shows what larger calibration sets would buy. (4) What a certificate cannot see (§6, §7). Under benchmark shift the error among accepted traces tracks the new task’s base error (Spearman 0.880.88): the target is exceeded in 40 of the 45 cells where the new task is harder and in none of the 27 where it is easier; under best-of-nn selection against the verifier it rises with nn past the target for several signals while the empirical failure frequency stays below δ\delta, because abstention absorbs the failures; the selected trace’s accuracy degrades.

Setting

Traces, labels, scores.

For a problem xx a model samples a CoT trace zz at temperature 0.80.8; Y=1Y=1 if its final answer matches the gold answer. A verifier signal is a map s⁡(z)∈ℝs(z)\in\mathbb{R}, fit on a training split and then frozen. We accept zz when s⁡(z)≥λs(z)\geq\lambda. The selective risk and coverage of a threshold are

R⁡(λ)\displaystyle R(\lambda) =P⁡(Y=0∣s⁡(Z)≥λ),\displaystyle=P\big(Y=0\mid s(Z)\geq\lambda\big),
C⁡(λ)\displaystyle C(\lambda) =P⁡(s⁡(Z)≥λ),\displaystyle=P\big(s(Z)\geq\lambda\big),

with R⁡(∞)=0R(\infty)=0. Let π0=P⁡(Y=0)\pi_{0}=P(Y=0). A procedure mapping a calibration set to λ^\hat{\lambda} is (α,δ)(\alpha,\delta)-valid if P⁡(R⁡(λ^)≤α)≥1−δP(R(\hat{\lambda})\leq\alpha)\geq 1-\delta. It fires when λ^<∞\hat{\lambda}<\infty, and Pfire=P⁡(λ^<∞)P_{\mathrm{fire}}=P(\hat{\lambda}<\infty). Our primary target is the boundary α=π0\alpha=\pi_{0}; we also report α∈{0.5​π0,0.75​π0}\alpha\in\{0.5\pi_{0},0.75\pi_{0}\} and α∈{0.05,0.10,0.20}\alpha\in\{0.05,0.10,0.20\}. At α=π0\alpha=\pi_{0} accepting everything is itself a correct answer, so this target measures whether the certificate can confirm what is true by construction; the targets below π0\pi_{0} are the non-vacuous ones, and even they can be loose in absolute terms (for the 33%-accurate model, 0.75​π00.75\pi_{0} is an error rate of 0.500.50).

Signals.

Each signal is a regularized logistic regression on a fixed feature set (Appendix B). Confidence: 5 summary statistics of the token log-probabilities of the trace. J-lens: 51 trajectory features (velocity, curvature, entropy and churn of the top-20 decoded tokens across reasoning steps) of residual-stream states decoded with the Jacobian lens of Gurnee et al., (2026). Logit lens: the same features with the Jacobian transport disabled (nostalgebraist,, 2020). Surface: geometric features of sentence embeddings (Reimers and Gurevych,, 2019) of the written steps. Probe: a linear probe on mid-depth residual vectors (mean over step positions, concatenated with the answer position). The first four have human-inspectable features; the probe does not.

The certificate.

Our main procedure is a Clopper–Pearson (CP) selective threshold (Clopper and Pearson,, 1934; Geifman and El-Yaniv,, 2017). Sort the nn calibration scores decreasingly, s(1)≥⋯≥s(n)s_{(1)}\geq\dots\geq s_{(n)}, and let eke_{k} count incorrect traces among the top kk. For a grid 𝒦⊂{10,…,n}\mathcal{K}\subset\{10,\dots,n\} of G≤20G\leq 20 equally spaced sizes fixed in advance, test the k−1k-1 traces strictly above s(k)s_{(k)}:

k^\displaystyle\hat{k} =max⁡{k∈𝒦:UCP​(ek−1,k−1,δ/G)≤α},\displaystyle=\max\{k\in\mathcal{K}:\ U_{\mathrm{CP}}(e_{k-1},k-1;\delta/G)\leq\alpha\}, (1)
λ^\displaystyle\hat{\lambda} =s(k^),\displaystyle=s_{(\hat{k})},

accept a test trace when s⁡(z)>λ^s(z)>\hat{\lambda}, and abstain (λ^=∞\hat{\lambda}=\infty) if the set is empty. UCP​(e,k,δ′)U_{\mathrm{CP}}(e,k;\delta^{\prime}) is the one-sided 1−δ′1-\delta^{\prime} CP upper limit, the 1−δ′1-\delta^{\prime} quantile of Beta⁡(e+1,k−e)\mathrm{Beta}(e+1,k-e). We use δ=0.10\delta=0.10.

Proposition 1 (Validity).

Let calibration traces be i.i.d. with continuous scores. Then rule (1) is (α,δ)(\alpha,\delta)-valid.

The proof (Appendix A) uses only that, conditional on s(k)=ts_{(k)}=t, the k−1k-1 traces above tt are i.i.d. from the law of (Y,s⁡(Z))(Y,s(Z)) given s⁡(Z)>ts(Z)>t, so ek−1∼Bin⁡(k−1,R⁡(t))e_{k-1}\sim\mathrm{Bin}(k-1,R(t)), and a union bound over 𝒦\mathcal{K}. Implementations often count the boundary trace as well, testing (ek,k)(e_{k},k) and accepting s≥λ^s\geq\hat{\lambda}; that variant needs P⁡(Y=0∣s⁡(Z)=t)≥R⁡(t)P(Y=0\mid s(Z)=t)\geq R(t) for all tt and is compared in Appendix E.

Alternatives.

(i) The same construction with the CP limit replaced by the Hoeffding–Bentkus p-value (Bates et al.,, 2021; Bentkus,, 2004; Angelopoulos et al.,, 2025) or a mixture betting e-value (Waudby-Smith and Ramdas,, 2024), on the same grid with the same split. (ii) Conformal selection (Jin and Candès,, 2023): p-values pj=(1+#{i:Yi=0,si≥sj})/(n0+1)p_{j}=(1+\#\{i:Y_{i}=0,\,s_{i}\geq s_{j}\})/(n_{0}+1) against the n0n_{0} incorrect calibration traces, then Benjamini–Hochberg (Benjamini and Hochberg,, 1995) at level α\alpha, which controls the false discovery rate among accepted traces. Conformal risk control (Angelopoulos et al.,, 2024) does not apply directly, since selective error is not monotone in λ\lambda.

Protocol.

11 1 Code, data and a one-command reproduction of every table and figure: https://github.com/ArjunBalaji79/certified-by-abstention-code.

Problems are split 30/40/30% into train (scorer fitting), calibration and test, by problem. Traces from one problem are dependent, so the unit of analysis is one trace per problem, redrawn in every replicate; calibration and test units are then exchangeable. Each configuration is evaluated over 1,000 replicates (200 resplits for each of 5 scorer seeds). The relative targets α=ρ​π0\alpha=\rho\pi_{0} use the base error rate of the training partition of the same seed, so every target is fixed before any calibration trace is seen; in the experimental sections π0\pi_{0} denotes this estimate (five values per model, spanning about ±0.02\pm 0.02), and the held-out base error serves only to classify targets as vacuous or not. For each we report mean coverage over all replicates, PfireP_{\mathrm{fire}}, and R^\hat{R}, the error rate among accepted test traces pooled over firing replicates (a coverage-weighted estimate of E⁡[R⁡(λ^)∣fire]E[R(\hat{\lambda})\mid\text{fire}]).

Three Structural Facts

The statements below have short proofs. We give them because they account for most of what we observe and, to our knowledge, have not been stated for verifier certification.

Lemma 1 (Certification floor).

Rule (1) can fire only if some k∈𝒦k\in\mathcal{K} satisfies k−1≥a0⋆k-1\geq a^{\star}_{0}, where

a0⋆​(α,δ/G):=⌈log⁡(G/δ)−log⁡(1−α)⌉,a^{\star}_{0}(\alpha,\delta/G):=\left\lceil\frac{\log(G/\delta)}{-\log(1-\alpha)}\right\rceil,

and this kk suffices only if the k−1k-1 calibration traces above s(k)s_{(k)} contain no error. Certifying an accepted set with ee errors requires k−1≥ae⋆k-1\geq a^{\star}_{e}, the smallest mm with UCP​(e,m,δ/G)≤αU_{\mathrm{CP}}(e,m;\delta/G)\leq\alpha, which increases with ee.

Proof.

UCP​(0,m,δ′)=1−δ′1/m≤αU_{\mathrm{CP}}(0,m;\delta^{\prime})=1-\delta^{\prime 1/m}\leq\alpha iff m≥log⁡δ′/log⁡(1−α)m\geq\log\delta^{\prime}/\log(1-\alpha). Monotonicity in ee follows from the stochastic ordering of Beta⁡(e+1,k−e)\mathrm{Beta}(e+1,k-e) in ee. ∎

At α=δ=0.10\alpha=\delta=0.10, G=20G=20 the floor is a0⋆=51a_{0}^{\star}=51 error-free traces above the threshold. For a model with π0=0.0886\pi_{0}=0.0886 calibrated on 74 problems (our Qwen3-8B cell) at α=π0\alpha=\pi_{0}, the floor is 58: a score with AUC near 0.60.6 must place none of about seven calibration errors among the 58 traces above the threshold, 78% of the calibration set. Figure 1 plots a⋆a^{\star} for accepted sets with error fraction 00, α/4\alpha/4 and α/2\alpha/2: at half the target, α=0.10\alpha=0.10 needs about 195 accepted calibration points, more than any calibration set here; dropping the Bonferroni grid (dashed) lowers the floor by a factor of about 2.32.3.

Proposition 2 (Lattice condition for conformal selection).

Let p1,…,pmp_{1},\dots,p_{m} be conformal p-values against n0n_{0} calibration nulls, with empirical c.d.f. F^m\hat{F}_{m}. BH at level α\alpha makes either no rejection or at least ⌈m/(α⁡(n0+1))⌉\lceil m/(\alpha(n_{0}+1))\rceil rejections, and it rejects if and only if

∃k∈{1,…,n0+1}:F^m​(kn0+1)≥kα⁡(n0+1).\exists\,k\in\{1,\dots,n_{0}+1\}:\quad\hat{F}_{m}\!\Big(\frac{k}{n_{0}+1}\Big)\ \geq\ \frac{k}{\alpha\,(n_{0}+1)}.

In particular, if a fraction q≥1/(α⁡(n0+1))q\geq 1/(\alpha(n_{0}+1)) of test traces outscores every calibration null, BH rejects.

The proof (Appendix A) uses only that conformal p-values lie on the lattice {k/(n0+1)}\{k/(n_{0}+1)\}; the same granularity governs the finite-calibration behaviour of BH with empirical null p-values analysed by Mary and Roquain, (2022), whose FDR bounds are exact when α⁡(n0+1)/m\alpha(n_{0}+1)/m is an integer and whose power analysis likewise needs n0≳m/max⁡(1,k)n_{0}\gtrsim m/\max(1,k) for kk detectable alternatives. With n0=25n_{0}=25 and α=0.10\alpha=0.10, BH must accept at least 38.5%38.5\% of the test set at once or nothing. The requirement n0≳1/(α​q)n_{0}\gtrsim 1/(\alpha q) is perverse for verification: it is a lower bound on the number of calibration errors, it grows as the target tightens, and a more accurate model both forces a tighter non-vacuous target and supplies fewer errors.

Proposition 3 (Validity by abstention).

If a procedure is (α,δ)(\alpha,\delta)-valid and fires with probability Pfire>0P_{\mathrm{fire}}>0, then

P⁡(R⁡(λ^)>α|fire)≤min⁡{1,δ/Pfire},P\big(R(\hat{\lambda})>\alpha\ \big|\ \text{fire}\big)\ \leq\ \min\{1,\ \delta/P_{\mathrm{fire}}\},

and for Pfire≤δP_{\mathrm{fire}}\leq\delta this is attained: there are (α,δ)(\alpha,\delta)-valid procedures whose every issued certificate is wrong.

Proof.

R⁡(∞)=0R(\infty)=0, so {R(λ^)>α}⊆{fire}\{R(\hat{\lambda})>\alpha\}\subseteq\{\text{fire}\} and the bound follows on dividing by PfireP_{\mathrm{fire}}. For attainment take any distribution with π0>α\pi_{0}>\alpha and the procedure that ignores the data, accepts everything with probability Pfire≤δP_{\mathrm{fire}}\leq\delta, and otherwise abstains. ∎

Proposition 3 says nothing against validity: validity is a statement about the calibration draw, abstentions included, whereas an operator acts only on certificates that are issued. When Pfire≤δP_{\mathrm{fire}}\leq\delta the guarantee is compatible with every issued certificate being wrong, a second sense, beyond α≥π0\alpha\geq\pi_{0}, in which it can be vacuous. The statement is elementary, and that is the point: certificates are reported by coverage averaged over calibration draws, or by error averaged with empty certificates counted as zero, and neither statistic can expose this regime; PfireP_{\mathrm{fire}} and the error of issued certificates do.

Attainability

Data.

Seven models (Qwen3.5-0.8B/4B, Qwen3-1.7B/4B/8B, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, OLMo-3-7B) generate 2–4 traces per GSM8K test problem (Cobbe et al.,, 2021) under a plain two-shot prompt: 295–1,387 usable traces over 167–395 problems per model, hence 67–158 calibration problems. Accuracy ranges from 0.330.33 to 0.910.91.

The boundary target.

Table 1 reports the certificate at α=π0\alpha=\pi_{0} and at 0.75​π00.75\pi_{0}. The boundary target sits at the edge of vacuity, so it is sensitive to the estimate that defines it: the training-partition π0\pi_{0} lies above the held-out base error by 0.010.01–0.040.04 for three models, below it by 0.010.01–0.030.03 for two, and within 0.0050.005 for two, and coverage at this target moves accordingly. Mean coverage conceals a bimodal outcome: the certificate either abstains or accepts a large set (32–86% of test traces given firing), and PfireP_{\mathrm{fire}} ranges from 0.020.02 to 0.960.96 across the 21 pairs. When the certificate fires, R^\hat{R} is 0.530.53–1.071.07 of the target, close to 11 for weak signals, which fire by accepting almost everything. The probe covers more than confidence and more than the J-lens signal in all seven models (geometric-mean ratios 1.81.8 and 3.33.3; sign test p=0.016p=0.016 for each, both significant under BH at 0.10 over the six secondary comparisons of this section and §6); in absolute terms its coverage exceeds confidence’s by up to 0.330.33 and the J-lens signal’s by up to 0.550.55. Confidence covers more than the J-lens signal in six of seven models (ratio 1.91.9, p=0.125p=0.125).

Non-vacuous targets.

At 0.75​π00.75\pi_{0}, which lies below the held-out base error in every cell, the picture is stark: Pfire≤δP_{\mathrm{fire}}\leq\delta for 15 of 21 pairs, mean coverage reaches 10%10\% for 2 of 21 (confidence and the probe on Qwen3.5-4B, 0.110.11 and 0.390.39), and the probe’s advantage widens (ratios 3.13.1 over confidence and 8.58.5 over the J-lens signal). Over all targets below the boundary (Appendix Table 5), 10%10\% coverage is reached by 3 of 21 pairs, the probe on Qwen3.5-4B and on Qwen3-1.7B and confidence on Qwen3.5-4B; two more, confidence and the probe on Qwen3.5-0.8B, reach it at the boundary target, which on that model lies below the held-out base error. At α=0.05\alpha=0.05 every signal has coverage below 0.1%0.1\%, as Lemma 1 predicts: a0⋆=104a_{0}^{\star}=104 error-free traces above the threshold exceeds four of the seven calibration sets and is two thirds of the largest.

Conformal selection.

At level α=π0\alpha=\pi_{0} BH conformal selection makes no rejection in 74% of replicates on average (Appendix Table 6). The lattice minimum of Proposition 2 ranges from 2% of the test set (Qwen3.5-0.8B, with 108 calibration errors) to 69% (Qwen3-4B), and for Qwen3-8B it exceeds the test set, so no rejection is possible. The condition also explains the one success: on Qwen3.5-0.8B, whose calibration sets contain 108 errors, BH rejects in 79–100% of replicates. The binding quantity is the number of calibration nulls, which for a correctness verifier is the number of calibration errors: 6–24 here for six of seven models, against the hundreds of nulls behind the power reported by Gui et al., (2024).

Is Low Coverage the Bound’s Fault?

No. For fixed kk the error count is binomial, a family with monotone likelihood ratio, so the binomial test behind the CP limit is uniformly most powerful among non-randomized tests at its size (Karlin–Rubin); Appendix Table 4 confirms that neither a Hoeffding–Bentkus nor a betting bound exceeds CP in any of the 21 cells.

What does cost coverage is the Bonferroni grid. A walk that tests every size at the full δ\delta, starting at the first size that passes, raises mean coverage from 0.210.21 to 0.430.43 but has no validity proof, since its start is chosen by the data; the textbook fixed-sequence walk from the strictest threshold (Bauer,, 1991) never fires for α<1−δ1/9=0.23\alpha<1-\delta^{1/9}=0.23 (Lemma 1). Section 5 resolves this.

Conditional Failure With Known Risk

Real test sets are too small to tell whether an issued certificate is wrong, so we simulate a Gaussian score model (incorrect scores N⁡(0,1)N(0,1), correct scores N⁡(μ,1)N(\mu,1) with μ\mu set by the AUC), where R⁡(λ)R(\lambda) is known, at sizes matched to four of our cells, 20,000 calibration draws each (Appendix Table 7 and Figure 5). At α=0.75​π0\alpha=0.75\pi_{0} with π0=0.16\pi_{0}=0.16, AUC 0.820.82, n=154n=154 (the Qwen3.5-4B probe regime), rule (1) fires in 56%56\% of draws and an issued certificate is wrong with probability 0.0030.003. At AUC 0.710.71 and α=0.5​π0\alpha=0.5\pi_{0} it fires in 0.5%0.5\% of draws and is wrong in 52%52\% of them; at π0=0.22\pi_{0}=0.22, AUC 0.760.76, n=78n=78 and the same target it fires in 0.4%0.4\% and is wrong in 69%69\%. In every setting the unconditional failure probability is at most 0.0030.003, more than thirty times below δ\delta. The failures are not gross: among failing draws the median R⁡(λ^)/αR(\hat{\lambda})/\alpha is 1.041.04–1.121.12 and the 90th percentile 1.131.13–1.281.28 in the seven settings with at least 29 failures; the eighth fires twice in 20,000 draws, both times wrong, at 1.541.54 and 1.631.63 (Appendix Table 7). They need not stay mild: under best-of-32 selection the error among accepted traces reaches 1.121.12–1.521.52 of the target in three of four firing pairs while the failure frequency stays below δ\delta (§7). Validity bounds the unconditional failure probability; the operator experiences the conditional one; abstention reconciles the two (Proposition 3).

Score Quality, Not Model Quality

One might expect better models to be harder to certify, since a non-vacuous α\alpha lies below π0\pi_{0}. Across the seven models, coverage at α=π0\alpha=\pi_{0} instead tracks the score’s test AUC (Spearman +0.79+0.79, p=0.036p=0.036, for both probe and confidence) more than model accuracy (−0.43-0.43 and −0.39-0.39, both ns). With seven models this is descriptive; budgets should be planned from the verifier’s AUC and Lemma 1.

Why the probe wins.

The probe’s advantage could be information the readable features cannot express, or better estimation of the same information. A cross-fitted reconstruction of the probe score from the 119 readable features (Appendix C) has mean held-out AUC 0.630.63 against 0.750.75 for the probe, and the residual has mean AUC 0.660.66 (0.590.59–0.720.72 across models), so the edge is not linearly recoverable from the readable features and the coverage gap reflects information rather than tuning, at least at these training sizes.

A Floor-Started Fixed-Sequence Certificate

Rule (1) pays for a Bonferroni split because its thresholds are order statistics of the calibration scores, so the hypotheses it tests are random. Learn-then-Test (Angelopoulos et al.,, 2025) already contains the remedy for a fixed grid: fixed-sequence testing of the grid hypotheses controls the family-wise error with no split and no monotonicity requirement. Two choices separate that recipe from a usable verifier certificate. The thresholds must be fixed without calibration data, which we do from the training split; and the walk must begin where certification is possible at all, since sizes below the floor of Lemma 1 cannot certify and a walk that begins there stops at once. FS-floor is fixed-sequence Learn-then-Test with these two choices and a start constant cc.

Procedure (FS-floor).

Let λ1>⋯>λJ\lambda_{1}>\dots>\lambda_{J} be the 1−qj1-q_{j} quantiles of the scorer’s training-split scores for accept fractions qj∈{0.02,0.04,…,1}q_{j}\in\{0.02,0.04,\dots,1\}. Let j0j_{0} be the first jj with qj​n≥c​a0⋆​(α,δ)q_{j}\,n\geq c\,a_{0}^{\star}(\alpha,\delta). For j=j0,j0+1,…j=j_{0},j_{0}+1,\dots let NjN_{j} and EjE_{j} count calibration traces and errors with s≥λjs\geq\lambda_{j}, and reject Hj:R⁡(λj)>αH_{j}:R(\lambda_{j})>\alpha when the exact binomial p-value P{Bin(Nj,α)≤Ej}P\{\mathrm{Bin}(N_{j},\alpha)\leq E_{j}\} is at most δ\delta. Stop at the first non-rejection and return the last rejected λj\lambda_{j}, or abstain if there is none.

Proposition 4.

FS-floor is (α,δ)(\alpha,\delta)-valid for any score distribution.

Proof.

The grid, the order and j0j_{0} depend only on the training split and nn, so each HjH_{j} is a fixed hypothesis, and given NjN_{j}, Ej∼Bin⁡(Nj,R⁡(λj))E_{j}\sim\mathrm{Bin}(N_{j},R(\lambda_{j})), so its p-value is valid. A false certification requires rejecting the first true HjH_{j} in the order, which has probability at most δ\delta (Bauer,, 1991). No monotonicity of RR is used. ∎

Choosing cc and the grid.

The constant cc sets how far above the zero-error floor the walk begins. Starting at the floor itself (c=1c=1) makes the first test intolerant of a single error, and on real data at α=π0\alpha=\pi_{0} that covers less than rule (1) (0.130.13 against 0.210.21). We therefore choose c∈{1,1.5,2,3,4}c\in\{1,1.5,2,3,4\} per cell before calibration: we simulate the Gaussian score model of §4.2 at the training split’s out-of-fold AUC, its base error rate and nn, and take the cc with the largest simulated coverage. The choice uses no calibration data, so Proposition 4 is untouched, and the Gaussian assumption affects only power. The grid is cross-fitted in the same spirit: its quantiles come from out-of-fold scores of the training problems, since in-sample scores are optimistic for the scorer. Appendix Table 8 and Figure 4 report every fixed cc, the in-sample grid and the per-model curves.

Results.

Table 2 compares FS-floor with rule (1). In simulation the failure probability is at most 0.0550.055 against δ=0.10\delta=0.10 for every cc and setting. At the chosen cc, coverage is 2.02.0–8.3×8.3\times that of rule (1) in the five settings where the latter fires in more than 1%1\% of draws, and 15×15\times in the one where it fires in 1%1\%; and PfireP_{\mathrm{fire}} rises from 0.110.11 to 0.400.40 in the AUC-0.710.71 regime; the probability that an issued certificate is wrong is 0.060.06–0.110.11 in the four settings where PfireP_{\mathrm{fire}} is at least 0.40.4 and grows as PfireP_{\mathrm{fire}} falls, as Proposition 3 predicts. FS-floor does not control this conditional failure, which validity alone does not guarantee; by raising PfireP_{\mathrm{fire}} it tightens the bound δ/Pfire\delta/P_{\mathrm{fire}}. On the real cells FS-floor covers more than rule (1) in all 21 pairs at all three targets. At α=0.75​π0\alpha=0.75\pi_{0} mean coverage rises from 0.0510.051 to 0.1630.163 and PfireP_{\mathrm{fire}} from 0.100.10 to 0.280.28, the number of pairs with Pfire≤δP_{\mathrm{fire}}\leq\delta falls from 15 to 4, and 11 pairs reach 10%10\% coverage against 2; at α=π0\alpha=\pi_{0} coverage rises from 0.2110.211 to 0.3900.390 and all 21 pairs reach 10%10\% against 14. Conditional on firing, R^/α\hat{R}/\alpha has median 0.800.80 at α=π0\alpha=\pi_{0} and 0.940.94 at 0.75​π00.75\pi_{0}, against 0.760.76 and 0.840.84 for rule (1): a procedure that abstains less certifies sets closer to the target, as it should. Two cheap baselines locate the gain (Appendix Table 9): shrinking the Bonferroni grid of rule (1) to G=5G=5 raises mean coverage at 0.75​π00.75\pi_{0} only from 0.050.05 to 0.070.07, and the floor start alone, a single fixed threshold tested at level δ\delta, reaches 0.100.10, and the walk 0.160.16. The simulation that chooses cc also predicts PfireP_{\mathrm{fire}} before any calibration label is seen; the forecast is rough (mean absolute error 0.100.10 against a mean PfireP_{\mathrm{fire}} of 0.280.28 at 0.75​π00.75\pi_{0}) but ranks the 21 pairs well (Spearman 0.700.70), so an operator can tell before labelling whether a certificate is likely to fire. The floor remains binding: no non-randomized procedure on this statistic can certify with fewer than a0⋆​(α,δ)a_{0}^{\star}(\alpha,\delta) accepted points, and mean coverage at 0.75​π00.75\pi_{0} stays at 0.160.16. Figure 2 shows what larger budgets buy in the Gaussian model: at AUC 0.760.76 the certificate fires in most draws from about 200 problems and covers half the traces from about 500; at AUC 0.660.66 even 3,000 problems certify fewer than half. FS-floor’s advantage is concentrated below a few hundred problems.

Shift

We freeze the GSM8K-trained scorer and the GSM8K-calibrated threshold (α=π0\alpha=\pi_{0} of GSM8K) and apply them to the same model’s traces on ARC-Challenge (Clark et al.,, 2018), StrategyQA (Geva et al.,, 2021), CommonsenseQA (Talmor et al.,, 2019) and three BIG-Bench-Hard logic tasks (Suzgun et al.,, 2023): 72 (model, benchmark, signal) cells. Exchangeability fails by construction (Tibshirani et al.,, 2019; Barber et al.,, 2023).

Every one of the 72 cells fires in some replicates. In 40 of them R^\hat{R} exceeds the target, by up to 0.280.28, and the split is clean: the target is exceeded in 40 of the 45 cells where the new task is harder than the target and in none of the 27 where it is easier. The error among accepted traces is a median 0.940.94 of the new task’s base error, so off-distribution the accepted set is barely better than accepting everything; Appendix Figure 6 and Table 10 show every cell. Across cells R^\hat{R} tracks the new task’s base error (Spearman 0.880.88), and the remaining benefit shrinks as the score’s AUC drops (Spearman 0.420.42; all p<10−3p<10^{-3}, nominal since cells cluster within models).

Selection Pressure

A deployed verifier is an optimization target: candidates are sampled and the top-scoring one is kept. Marginal conformal guarantees can fail under data-driven selection (Jin and Ren,, 2025), and proxy scores are overoptimized by best-of-nn (BoN) (Gao et al.,, 2023). We measure the dose-response for verifier certificates.

Design.

For Qwen3.5-4B and Qwen3-4B we sample up to 64 traces per problem on GSM8K problems unused elsewhere in this paper, so the frozen scorers have never seen them; 149 and 243 problems retain at least 32 usable traces, and analyses use 32 per problem. Pressure runs over n∈{1,2,4,…,32}n\in\{1,2,4,\dots,32\}, up to log⁡n−(n−1)/n=2.5\log n-(n-1)/n=2.5 nats from the base policy (Beirami et al.,, 2025). In the naive arm the threshold is calibrated on unpressured traces from half of the problems and applied to BoN-selected traces of the other half. The target is the model’s GSM8K training-partition base error from §4 (0.160.16 and 0.100.10), fixed before any pressure problem was drawn; the sample base errors of the pressure problems are 0.200.20 and 0.110.11, so both targets are non-vacuous there. In the corrected arm calibration traces are selected by the same BoN rule, restoring exchangeability conditional on selection (Jin and Ren,, 2025). We use 1,000 resplits.

Error among accepted rises with nn.

Calibration sets here are 74 and 122 problems, half of the pressure problems, and the targets are non-vacuous, so PfireP_{\mathrm{fire}} is low: 0.140.14 for the probe and 0.030.03 for confidence on Qwen3.5-4B, 0.090.09 and 0.050.05 for confidence and the probe on Qwen3-4B, and at most 0.020.02 otherwise. Conditional on firing (Figure 3; Appendix Table 11 and Figure 7), R^/α\hat{R}/\alpha rises from 0.870.87 to 1.521.52 for the probe and from 0.780.78 to 1.121.12 for confidence on Qwen3-4B, and from 0.920.92 to 1.251.25 for confidence on Qwen3.5-4B. The exception is the probe on Qwen3.5-4B (0.70→0.690.70\to 0.69), the one pair for which BoN improves the policy monotonically. The naive arm breaks exchangeability between calibration and deployment, so Proposition 1 promises nothing for it; what happens empirically is that the fraction of replicates whose test error among accepted exceeds α\alpha stays below δ\delta in every cell (at most 0.0560.056), because most replicates accept nothing.

Overoptimization.

The accuracy of the BoN-selected trace (Figure 3, accuracy panels) peaks at small nn and then falls for several signals. On Qwen3-4B the probe loses 3.33.3 points from its peak at n=2n=2 and confidence 1.81.8 from n=4n=4; on Qwen3.5-4B the surface signal loses 5.75.7 and the logit lens 2.62.6, while the probe gains 7.77.7 monotonically. No signal is uniformly safe; the bands are wide and we make no confirmatory claim about the ranking. Regardless of ranking, a bound on error among accepted traces, calibrated before optimization, says nothing about whether selecting on the score still improves the policy.

The correction costs coverage.

Selection-conditional calibration restores the exchangeability that Proposition 1 needs, so the corrected arm is valid at every nn, but at n=32n=32 its mean coverage falls to 0.0050.005 or below in three of the four principal cells. Only the strongest scorer benefits (probe on Qwen3.5-4B, 0.09→0.220.09\to 0.22), because BoN has lowered that policy’s error to 0.120.12, below the 0.160.16 target.

Related Work

Distribution-free selection and risk control.

Selective classification with binomial certificates goes back to El-Yaniv and Wiener, (2010) and Geifman and El-Yaniv, (2017); RCPS (Bates et al.,, 2021), Learn-then-Test (Angelopoulos et al.,, 2025) and conformal risk control (Angelopoulos et al.,, 2024) generalize the risk and the search. Conformal p-values with BH give FDR-controlled selection (Bates et al.,, 2023; Jin and Candès,, 2023), applied to LLM outputs by Gui et al., (2024); Mohri and Hashimoto, (2024); Quach et al., (2024); these works show power at moderate to large calibration sizes, and we characterize the small-budget regime.

Verifier signals.

Confidence (Kadavath et al.,, 2022), hidden-state probes (Azaria and Mitchell,, 2023; Burns et al.,, 2023; Zhang et al.,, 2025), learned verifiers (Cobbe et al.,, 2021; Lightman et al.,, 2024) and lens readouts (nostalgebraist,, 2020; Belrose et al.,, 2023; Gurnee et al.,, 2026) are evaluated by ranking metrics; monitoring written CoT, which can be unfaithful (Turpin et al.,, 2023), is an active proposal (Korbak et al.,, 2025; Baker et al.,, 2025). We price readability in deployment terms.

Overoptimization.

Gao et al., (2023) characterize BoN and RL overoptimization of reward models; ensembles mitigate but do not remove it (Coste et al.,, 2024; Eisenstein et al.,, 2024). We study correctness verifiers with exact labels and ask what happens to a certificate; Jin and Ren, (2025) prove that selection breaks marginal conformal coverage and give the correction whose coverage cost we measure.

Limitations and Discussion

All models are open-weight decoders of at most 8B parameters; certification is on GSM8K with one prompt format and temperature 0.80.8. Scorers are fit on the 30% training partition, which for the most accurate model holds only 4–12 incorrect traces, so the readable signals’ AUCs, and the coverage gap to the probe, may narrow with more training errors. The best-of-nn results cover two models. Replicate-based uncertainty reflects resplitting on a fixed problem sample. The probe reconstruction is linear, so a non-linear readable reconstruction could narrow the gap.

We draw four practical conclusions. Report PfireP_{\mathrm{fire}} next to coverage, and treat (α,δ)(\alpha,\delta)-validity as uninformative about issued certificates when Pfire≤δP_{\mathrm{fire}}\leq\delta. Fix thresholds before calibration and start testing at the floor. Budget calibration labels from Lemma 1 and the verifier’s AUC before collecting them; accepted traces are only a fraction of the labelled ones. Do not read a valid certificate as evidence that the verifier is safe to optimize against or to move to a new task: in our data the error among accepted traces followed the task and the optimizer, not the certificate.

AI use statement

We used a large language model coding assistant throughout this work. It helped write and debug the analysis code, draft and edit the text and figures, and refine the experimental design, hypotheses, proofs of the statements in Section 3, data processing and interpretation of results. The research questions, design decisions and claims are the authors’; we checked every script and every line of the paper, all tables and figures are regenerated by script from the released result files, and we take responsibility for the final content.

Boundary-included variant.

If the rule also counts the boundary trace, testing (ek,k)(e_{k},k) and accepting s≥S(k)s\geq S_{(k)}, then ek=ek−1+Be_{k}=e_{k-1}+B where, given S(k)=tS_{(k)}=t, B∼Bern⁡(r⁡(t))B\sim\mathrm{Bern}(r(t)) with r⁡(t)=P⁡(Y=0∣S=t)r(t)=P(Y=0\mid S=t), independent of ek−1e_{k-1}. If r⁡(t)≥R⁡(t)r(t)\geq R(t) then eke_{k} is stochastically larger than Bin⁡(k,R⁡(t))\mathrm{Bin}(k,R(t)), and since UCP​(⋅,k,δ′)U_{\mathrm{CP}}(\cdot,k;\delta^{\prime}) is increasing in its first argument the same bound holds. The condition is implied by a monotone likelihood ratio between the score distributions of incorrect and correct traces. Without it the variant can be anti-conservative by at most the contribution of one observation. Table 6 compares the two rules on our data. ∎

Proposition 2.

Write N=n0+1N=n_{0}+1. Every conformal p-value lies in {1/N,…,1}\{1/N,\dots,1\}. BH rejects the RR smallest p-values, R=max⁡{r:p(r)≤α​r/m}R=\max\{r:p_{(r)}\leq\alpha r/m\}, with R=0R=0 if the set is empty. If R≥1R\geq 1 then 1/N≤p(R)≤α​R/m1/N\leq p_{(R)}\leq\alpha R/m, so R≥m/(α​N)R\geq m/(\alpha N), which gives the first claim. For the equivalence: if m​F^m​(k/N)≥k​m/(α​N)m\hat{F}_{m}(k/N)\geq km/(\alpha N) for some kk, put r=m​F^m​(k/N)r=m\hat{F}_{m}(k/N); then p(r)≤k/N≤α​r/mp_{(r)}\leq k/N\leq\alpha r/m, so R≥r≥1R\geq r\geq 1. Conversely, if p(r)≤α​r/mp_{(r)}\leq\alpha r/m for some r≥1r\geq 1, let k=N​p(r)k=Np_{(r)}; then m​F^m​(k/N)≥r≥p(r)​m/α=k​m/(α​N)m\hat{F}_{m}(k/N)\geq r\geq p_{(r)}m/\alpha=km/(\alpha N). The last claim is the case k=1k=1, since F^m​(1/N)\hat{F}_{m}(1/N) is the fraction of test traces that outscore every calibration null. ∎

Appendix B Signals, Data and Compute

Generation.

Plain-text two-shot prompts with exemplars from the GSM8K training split; temperature 0.80.8, top-pp 0.950.95, at most 640 new tokens; 2–4 samples per problem. A trace is usable if it contains a parseable final answer. For multiple-choice and yes/no benchmarks answers are parsed with a style-anchored rule, because base models frequently continue writing past their answer. Models: Qwen3.5-0.8B and Qwen3.5-4B (Qwen Team,, 2026), Qwen3-1.7B, Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B (Yang et al.,, 2025), Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct (Yang et al.,, 2024) and Olmo-3-1025-7B (Team Olmo,, 2025), all under their published open-weight licences. The Jacobian lens and its pre-fitted per-model lenses are the public release accompanying Gurnee et al., (2026).

Features.

Residual-stream states are read at the last token of each reasoning step, at every second layer, in a teacher-forced pass. J-lens and logit lens: 51 features each, namely step-to-step cosine velocity, curvature, path length, tortuosity and terminal alignment of the decoded top-20 token distributions, plus entropy, churn and the rate of “silent” concepts (decoded but never written). Surface: 9 geometric features of all-mpnet-base-v2 embeddings of the written step text. Confidence: 5 statistics of the token log-probabilities. Length: 3 trace-length features, included only in the 119-feature readable set of Appendix C. Probe: residual vectors at layer round⁡(L/2)\mathrm{round}(L/2), mean over step positions concatenated with the answer position (2​dmodel2d_{\mathrm{model}} dimensions).

Scorers.

Standardization followed by ℓ2\ell_{2}-regularized logistic regression (C=1.0C=1.0 for the four readable signals, C=0.01C=0.01 for the probe), fit on all traces of the 30% training problems, separately for 5 seeds of the train split, and frozen. The target levels α=ρ​π0\alpha=\rho\,\pi_{0} use π0\pi_{0} estimated on the training partition of the same seed.

Compute.

Generation and feature extraction ran on single A100 GPUs from a commercial cloud provider, for a total cost of roughly US$50. All certificate analyses run on a laptop CPU from the cached per-trace scores. Code, data and a script that regenerates every table and figure are in the anonymized repository https://github.com/ArjunBalaji79/certified-by-abstention-code (about 70 minutes end to end on a laptop CPU).

Best-of-nn details.

The certificate arms draw best-of-nn subsets by Monte Carlo from 32 traces per problem; the accuracy curves use the closed-form rank weights. Exact duplicate traces (6% and 15% of samples for the two models) make score ties common; ties are broken by a fixed random key, and tied traces share a label.

Statistics.

For each configuration we report mean coverage over all replicates, the firing probability PfireP_{\mathrm{fire}}, and R^\hat{R}, the error rate among accepted test traces pooled over firing replicates. We do not average per-replicate error with empty certificates counted as zero, since that average is dominated by abstentions. The comparison of J-lens and confidence coverage, the probe residual analysis and the best-of-nn sweep were specified before the corresponding data were collected; statistics conditional on firing, the shift analysis by task difficulty and FS-floor were developed afterwards.

Appendix C Probe Reconstruction

The probe’s advantage could be information that the readable features cannot express, or better estimation of the same information. We reconstruct the probe score from the 119 readable features by a ridge regression fit on out-of-fold probe scores of the training problems, choose every regularization constant by grouped cross-validation on those problems, and evaluate on held-out problems (below). The reconstruction has mean AUC 0.630.63 across the seven models, no better than the readable logistic regression (0.650.65) and well below the probe (0.750.75); the residual, probe minus reconstruction, keeps mean AUC 0.660.66 and lies between 0.590.59 and 0.720.72 on every model; and as a certificate signal the reconstruction buys the readable signals’ coverage, not the probe’s. The probe’s edge is therefore not linearly expressible in the readable features, and the coverage gap reflects information rather than tuning, at least at these training sizes: cross-validating the readable scorers’ regularization moves their AUC by 0.020.02. (Regressing on in-sample probe scores instead gives residual AUC 0.540.54; the next paragraph explains why.)

For each of 5 splits by problem (30% training), we fit the probe (2​dmodel2d_{\mathrm{model}}-dimensional mid-depth residual vectors at the step and answer positions, 2,0482{,}048–8,1928{,}192 across models, C∈{10−3,10−2,10−1}C\in\{10^{-3},10^{-2},10^{-1}\}) and the readable logistic regression (119 features, C∈{10−2,…,10}C\in\{10^{-2},\dots,10\}) on the training problems with CC chosen by 5-fold grouped cross-validation, obtain out-of-fold probe scores on the training problems, and fit a ridge regression (standardized features, λ∈{0.1,…,100}\lambda\in\{0.1,\dots,100\} by the same cross-validation) from the readable features to those out-of-fold scores. All quantities in Table 3 are evaluated on the held-out problems. An in-sample variant of this test, which regresses on the probe’s in-sample scores on the training problems, is misleading: a 2​dmodel2d_{\mathrm{model}}-dimensional probe separates its training data almost perfectly, so that regression learns a readable predictor of the label rather than of the probe, and its residual (AUC 0.540.54) removes the label-correlated part of the probe by construction. The certificate columns rerun rule (1) on the held-out problems (calibration/test split 4:34{:}3, 200 resplits per training split) with each score as the signal.
